narrative:
Based on your profile, the model estimates a 47 in 100 chance that you will leave, and this was treated as a high enough retention risk to deny the promotion. This is not a certainty about your intentions; it is a warning signal that the promotion decision is being made through a leaving-risk lens.

The strongest factor in the prediction was your overall years of experience. Because you have only one to five years of experience—a range shared by about half of employees predicted to stay—this factor actually pushed the estimate toward staying. The second most influential factor was that you have received other job opportunities while in this role. Only about 23% of employees predicted to stay reported such opportunities, so this pushed toward leaving. The third factor was work–life balance. You described balancing work and personal life as difficult, while only about 9% of employees predicted to stay reported that level of difficulty; this also increased the leaving risk.

Given this, the organization should consider whether the promotion process is being overly driven by leave-risk rather than current performance, and should discuss concrete retention steps with you: how to manage external opportunities, improve work–life balance, and clarify career progression. You may want to document your contributions, seek feedback on promotion criteria, and raise workload or flexibility concerns directly. Your relatively short experience was not working against you here; the main concerns are opportunity pull and work–life strain.
